summary: Reviews the Initial Connection Protocol after RFC 165. An ICP committee had aimed for something that works quickly with few changes, and interviewed people with objections, ending in a compromise. The author notes the committee had no time to think about alternatives.

plainLanguage.summary: After a hurry-up fix, one person asks whether it was the best plan, since no one had time to think about other ideas.

questions: what is wrong with the icp in rfc 165
how was the icp committee formed
subtitle: A simpler alternative to the rushed Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: The ICP committee hurried to minimize changes to an existing protocol. As a result, the Initial Connection Protocol is more complex than necessary, requiring multiple steps and having potential race conditions.
tldr.mechanism: An alternative approach uses simple commands: ISC/ASC/RSC for simplex connections and IDC/ADC/RDC for duplex connections. The server listens on one socket for connection requests rather than accepting connections on a separate socket and exchanging metadata.
tldr.outcome: Fewer message exchanges, no race conditions, and simpler state management, as long as the underlying Host-Host protocol is enhanced to support the commands.

today: RFC 197 is a design review from July 1971 of the Initial Connection Protocol. It represents an alternative that the author believed was superior but was not adopted at the time due to the committee's time constraints.

sections.title: Background on the ICP Committee
sections.content: RFC 197 reviews the Initial Connection Protocol after RFC 165. An ICP committee was formed before SJCC '71 with the goal of getting "something" working quickly with minimal changes to the existing protocol to minimize complaints. Those with objections to the current ICP were interviewed, and a compromise was reached in RFC 165. However, the committee lacked time to consider alternative approaches. This RFC attempts a simpler ICP design assuming the underlying Host-Host protocol could be enhanced with new commands, offering a design that the author hoped would inform the next Host-Host protocol version.
sections.plainLanguage: The first fix was a quick compromise. This note suggests: if we had time, here is what we would have done instead.

sections.title: The Proposed ICP Commands
sections.content: The alternative uses three commands for simplex connections: ISC (Initiate Simplex Connection), ASC (Accept Simplex Connection), and RSC (Refuse Simplex Connection). A user's NCP issues ISC with a server socket name L, user socket U, and byte size parameter X. The server responds with ASC (accepting with an assigned socket S) or RSC (refusing). For duplex connections, the commands are IDC (Initiate Duplex Connection), ADC (Accept Duplex Connection), and RDC (Refuse Duplex Connection), which work symmetrically with pairs of sockets and byte sizes. After the server accepts a connection, it immediately enters a connected state without requiring a separate ALL command.
sections.plainLanguage: Send: 'Connect to the logger'. Get back: 'OK, use this socket' or 'No'. Done. No extra steps.

sections.title: Why This Design Is Better
sections.content: The main advantage is minimization of dialog between user and server. In RFC 165, the user must establish a connection to the server's listening socket, choose a byte size, send an ALL command, exchange data, and then close the connection. In the proposed approach, the server socket L is used only as an address, not a socket to connect to, eliminating connection overhead. Race conditions (such as those described in RFC 143) do not arise because there is no negotiation phase. The server should be in a "Listening for ICP" state when ISC or IDC is received; if not, it refuses the request and does not queue ICP requests. Socket restrictions from RFC 165 (reserving U+2 and U+3) are eliminated, allowing any valid socket pair as long as they have opposite gender.
sections.plainLanguage: No back-and-forth. The listener just says yes or no. No hidden assumptions about which sockets are reserved. Simpler code, fewer bugs.
